body.heading: One substance, three behaviours
paragraphs: Everything around you is made of particles in constant motion, and temperature is really a measure of how energetically they move. In a solid, the particles are held in fixed positions by strong attractions; they cannot travel, only vibrate on the spot, which is why solids keep their own shape and volume.

Give the particles more energy and the attractions loosen. In a liquid they stay close but slide past one another, so a liquid keeps its volume but takes the shape of its container. Give them more energy still and they break free entirely: a gas's particles fly in straight lines, bouncing off each other and the walls, spreading to fill any space they are given.

body.heading: Changing state, step by step
paragraphs: Heating a solid melts it once its particles vibrate hard enough to escape their fixed positions. Keep heating the liquid and its fastest particles escape from the surface — evaporation — until, at boiling point, bubbles of gas form throughout the liquid. Cooling runs the film backwards: gas condenses to liquid, and liquid freezes to solid.

Notice what does not change: the particles themselves. Ice, water and steam are all H₂O. Melting and boiling are physical changes — rearrangements of movement, not new substances — which is why they can be reversed simply by cooling.

body.heading: Water, the odd one out
paragraphs: Most substances shrink steadily as they freeze, but water expands. Its molecules lock into an open, spaced-out crystal pattern in ice, so ice is less dense than liquid water and floats — which is why lakes freeze from the top down and fish can survive the winter underneath.

There is also a fourth state worth meeting: heat a gas hard enough and its atoms lose electrons, becoming a plasma. Lightning, the Sun and the glowing gas inside a neon sign are all plasma — by far the most common state of ordinary matter in the universe, even if it is rare in your kitchen.

description: Ice, water and steam are the same particles behaving differently — what changes between them is how much energy they have to move.
